title: The Worst-Done Part of Worship
hook: He said church singing was the worst-done part of worship. *So he wrote new songs.*
dateline: Isaac Watts · Died on this day, November 25, 1748 · Stoke Newington, England
summary: Isaac Watts died on November 25, 1748, leaving the church about 600 hymns.

story: The man was barely five feet tall, and after one bad fever he was never fully well again. He spent his last 36 years as a guest in other people's houses. On November 25, 1748, 278 years ago today, Isaac Watts died in Stoke Newington, outside London, in the home of the friends who had taken him in. He left the church about 600 hymns.

He was born in Southampton on July 17, 1674, into a Nonconformist family that worshipped outside the Church of England. His father had been jailed twice for his faith. Watts grew up loving words, and unhappy with how his church sang them.

There is a story, told later as “the tradition,” that the young Watts, home in Southampton around age 20, complained about the psalm-singing at his family's chapel and was told to write something better. His first hymn was the answer, the story goes, and the congregation asked for another, and another. Whether or not it happened that way, Watts said the same thing in print. “While we sing the Praises of our God in his Church,” he wrote in 1707, “we are employed in that part of Worship which of all others is the nearest a-kin to Heaven: and ‘tis pity that this of all others should be performed the worst upon Earth.”

So he set out to fix it. The chapels he knew sang rhymed versions of the Psalms. Watts wrote new songs in plain English about Jesus. *Hymns and Spiritual Songs* came out in 1707, with “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross” inside. In 1719 *The Psalms of David Imitated* reworked the old psalms “in the language of the New Testament.” Psalm 90 became “Our God, our help in ages past” (John Wesley changed the first word to “O” in 1738). Psalm 98 became “Joy to the World,” probably not written as a Christmas song at all.

Long before that, his body had given out. In 1712, ten years into his pastorate at the Mark Lane chapel in London, he fell seriously ill. Sir Thomas Abney invited him to his house in Hertfordshire to recover. Watts came for a week. He never left. He stayed on with Lady Abney and her family after Sir Thomas died, and moved with them to Abney House in Stoke Newington, where a plaque says he stayed from 1734 to 1748. Samuel Johnson wrote that Watts was “treated for thirty-six years with all the kindness that friendship could prompt.”
From that borrowed room he kept writing: sermons, a textbook on logic, and songs for children. Johnson admired a philosopher who would stop to make “a catechism for children in their fourth year.”

He died at 74, worn out slowly. His friends buried him in Bunhill Fields, the burial ground for London's Dissenters. On December 11, 1748, David Jennings preached to his old congregation about his death.

Watts never had a pulpit as big as his songs, or a house of his own. But God gave him a home, and gave the church the words. This December, someone will sing “Joy to the World” without knowing his name.

scripture.text: Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
scripture.note: Watts turned Psalm 90 into “Our God, our help in ages past.”

why: Every December, churches still sing “Joy to the World,” and around Easter “When I Survey the Wondrous Cross.” Both came from a sick, five-foot pastor living as a guest in a friend's house. God used him to teach English-speaking churches to sing the gospel in their own words.
